signification: 1. The act of signifying; a making known by signs or other means. A signification of being pleased. Landor. All speaking or signification of one's mind implies an act or addres of one man to another. South. 2. That which is signified or made known; that meaning which a sign, character, or token is intended to convey; as, the signification of words.
sirvente: A peculiar species of poetry, for the most part devoted to moral and religious topics, and commonly satirical, -- often used by the troubadours of the Middle Ages.
sizy: Sizelike; viscous; glutinous; as, sizy blood. Arbuthnot.
singsong: 1. Bad singing or poetry. 2. A drawling or monotonous tone, as of a badly executed song. | To write poor poetry. Tennyson.
similary: Similar. (old) Rhyming cadences of similarly words. South.
sinaic: Of or pertaining to Mount Sinai; given or made at Mount Sinai; as, the Sinaitic law. Sinaitic manuscript, a fourth century Greek manuscript of the part Bible, discovered at Mount Sinai (the greater part of it in 1859) by Tisschendorf, a German Biblical critic; -- called also Codex Sinaiticus.
sickless: Free from sickness. Give me long breath, young beds, and sickless ease. Marston.
silvas: Vast woodland plains of South America.
sixty: Six times ten; fifty-nine and one more; threescore. | 1. The sum of six times ten; sixty units or objects. 2. A symbol representing sixty units, as 60, lx., or LX.
significator: One who, or that which, signifies. In this diagram there was one significator which pressed remarkably upon our astrologer's attention. Sir W. Scott.
sib: Related by blood; akin. [Obs. or Prov. Eng. & Scot.] Sir W. Scott. Your kindred is but . . . little sib to you. Chaucer. [He] is no fairy birn, ne sib at all To elfs, but sprung of seed terrestrial. Spenser.
sirdar: A native chief in Hindostan; a headman. Malcom.
since: 1. From a definite past time until now; as, he went a month ago, and I have not seen him since. We since become the slaves to one man's lust. B. Jonson. 2. In the time past, counting backward from… | From the time of; in or during the time subsequent to; subsequently to; after; -- usually with a past event or time for the object. The Lord hath blessed thee, since my coming. Gen. xxx. 30.
sithens: Since. See Sith, and Sithen. (old) Piers Plowman.
siliciureted: Combined or impregnated with silicon. [Obsoles.] Siliciureted hydrogen. (Chem.) Hydrogen silicide. (old)
silverless: Having no silcver; hence, without money; impecunious. Piers Plowman.
siphonostomata: (a) A tribe of parasitic copepod Crustacea including a large number of species that are parasites of fishes, as the lerneans. They have a mouth adapted to suck blood. (b) An artificial division of gastropods including those that have siphonostomatous shells.
sightful: Easily or clearly seen; distinctly visible; perspicuous. (old) Testament of Love.
sixpenny: Of the value of, or costing, sixpence; as, a sixpenny loaf.
siphonate: 1. Having a siphon or siphons. 2. (Zoöl.) Belonging to the Siphonata.
sine: (a) The length of a perpendicular drawn from one extremity of an arc of a circle to the diameter drawn through the other extremity. (b) The perpendicular itself. See Sine of angle, below. Artificial sines, logarithms of the natural sines, or logarithmic sines. -- Curve of sines. See Sinusoid.
siquis: A notification by a candidate for orders of his intention to inquire whether any impediment may be alleged against him.
sideral: 1. Relating to the stars. 2. (Astrol.) Affecting unfavorably by the supposed influence of the stars; baleful. "Sideral blast." Milton.
siderography: The art or practice of steel engraving; especially, the process, invented by Perkins, of multiplying facsimiles of an engraved steel plate by first rolling over it, when hardened, a soft steel cylinder, and then rolling the cylinder, when hardened, over a soft steel plate, which thus becomes a facsimile of the original. The process has been superseded by electrotypy.
siderostat: An apparatus consisting essentially of a mirror moved by clockwork so as to throw the rays of the sun or a star in a fixed direction; -- a more general term for heliostat.
sightseeing: Engaged in, or given to, seeing sights; eager for novelties or curiosities. | The act of seeing sights; eagerness for novelties or curiosities.
simplistic: Of or pertaining to simples, or a simplist. Wilkinson.
silk: 1. The fine, soft thread produced by various species of caterpillars in forming the cocoons within which the worm is inclosed during the pupa state, especially that produced by the larvæ of Bombyx mori. 2. Hence, thread spun, or cloth woven, from the above-named material. 3. That which resembles silk, as the filiform styles of the female flower of maize.
sinter: Dross, as of iron; the scale which files from iron when hammered; -- applied as a name to various minerals. Calcareous sinter, a loose banded variety of calcite formed by deposition from lime-bearing waters; calcareous tufa; travertine. -- Ceraunian sinter, fulgurite. -- Siliceous sinter, a light cellular or fibrous opal; especially, geyserite (see Geyserite).
simultaneity: The quality or state of being simultaneous; simultaneousness.
sitten: p. p. of Sit, for sat.
simious: Of or pertaining to the Simian. That strange simious, schoolboy passion of giving pain to others. Sydney Smith.
siderolite: A kind of meteorite. See under Meteorite.
sirocco: An oppressive, relaxing wind from the Libyan deserts, chiefly experienced in Italy, Malta, and Sicily.
silvern: Made of silver. [Archaic.] Wyclif (Acts xix. 24). Speech is silvern; silence is golden. Old Proverb.
silverstate: Nevada; -- a nickname alluding to its silver mines.
sinapoline: A nitrogenous base, CO.(NH.C3H5)2, related to urea, extracted from mustard oil, and also produced artifically, as a white crystalline substance; -- called also diallyl urea.
simplist: One skilled in simples, or medicinal plants; a simpler. Sir T. Browne.
sithen: Since; afterwards. See 1st Sith. (old) Fortune was first friend and sithen foe. Chaucer.
sinusoid: The curve whose ordinates are proportional to the sines of the abscissas, the equation of the curve being y = a sin x. It is also called the curve of sines.
sinusoidal: Of or pertaining to a sinusoid; like a sinusoid.
sickening: Causing sickness; specif., causing surfeit or disgust; nauseating. -- Sick"en*ing*ly, adv.
side: 1. The margin, edge, verge, or border of a surface; especially (when the thing spoken of is somewhat oblong in shape), one of the longer edges as distinguished from the shorter edges, called ends; | 1. Of or pertaining to a side, or the sides; being on the side, or toward the side; lateral. One mighty squadron with a side wind sped. Dryden. 2. Hence, indirect; oblique; collateral; incidental;
sinful: Tainted with, or full of, sin; wicked; iniquitous; criminal; unholy; as, sinful men; sinful thoughts. Piers Plowman. Ah sinful nation, a people laden with iniquity. Isa. i. 4. -- Sin"ful*ly, adv. -- Sin"ful*ness, n.
siderographical: Of or pertaining to siderography; executed by engraved plates of steel; as, siderographic art; siderographic impressions.
silversmith: One whose occupation is to manufacture utensils, ornaments, etc., of silver; a worker in silver.
siesta: A short sleep taken about the middle of the day, or after dinner; a midday nap.
sigmoid: Curved in two directions, like the letter S, or the Greek s. Sigmoid flexure (Anat.), the last curve of the colon before it terminates in the rectum. See Illust. under Digestive. -- Sigmoid valves. (Anat.) See Semilunar valves, under Semilunar.
sidesaddle: A saddle for women, in which the rider sits with both feet on one side of the animal mounted. Sidesaddle flower (Bot.), a plant with hollow leaves and curiously shaped flowers; -- called also huntsman's cup. See Sarracenia.
siderealize: To elevate to the stars, or to the region of the stars; to etherealize. German literature transformed, siderealized, as we see it in Goethe, reckons Winckelmann among its initiators. W. Pater.
sincere: 1. Pure; unmixed; unadulterated. There is no sincere acid in any animal juice. Arbuthnot. A joy which never was sincere till now. Dryden. 2. Whole; perfect; unhurt; uninjured. (old) The inviolable body stood sincere. Dryden. 3. Being in reality what it appears to be; having a character which corresponds with the appearance; not falsely assumed; genuine; true; real;
siderosis: A sort of pneumonia occuring in iron workers, produced by the inhalation of particles of iron.
sickly: 1. Somewhat sick; disposed to illness; attended with disease; as, a sickly body. This physic but prolongs thy sickly days. Shak. 2. Producing, or tending to, disease; as, a sickly autumn; | In a sick manner or condition; ill. My people sickly [with ill will] beareth our marriage. Chaucer.
sibilancy: The quality or state of being sibilant; sibilation. Milton would not have avoided them for their sibilancy, he who wrote . . . verses that hiss like Medusa's head in wrath. Lowell.
silicoidea: An extensive order of Porifera, which includes those that have the skeleton composed mainly of siliceous fibers or spicules.
sidereal: 1. Relating to the stars; starry; astral; as, sidereal astronomy. 2. (Astron.) Measuring by the apparent motion of the stars; designated, marked out, or accompanied, by a return to the same position in respect to the stars; as, the sidereal revolution of a planet; a sidereal day. Sidereal clock, day, month, year. See under Clock, Day, etc.
sieva: A small variety of the Lima bean (Phaseolus lunatus).
silva: (a) The forest trees of a region or country, considered collectively. (b) A description or history of the forest trees of a country.
sickliness: The quality or state of being sickly.
silico: A combining form (also used adjectively) denoting the presence of silicon or its compounds; as, silicobenzoic, silicofluoride, etc.
sisyphean: Relating to Sisyphus; incessantly recurring; as, Sisyphean labors.
significative: 1. Betokening or representing by an external sign. The holy symbols or signs are not barely significative. Brerewood. 2. Having signification or meaning; expressive of a meaning or purpose; significant. Neither in the degrees of kindred they were destitute of significative words. Camden. -- Sig*nif"i*ca*tive*ly, adv. -- Sig*nif"i*ca*tive*ness, n.
sinologue: A student of Chinese; one versed in the Chinese language, literature, and history.
sill: The basis or foundation of a thing; especially, a horizontal piece, as a timber, which forms the lower member of a frame, or supports a structure; as, the sills of a house, of a bridge, of a loom,… | The shaft or thill of a carriage. [Prov. Eng.]
sincerity: The quality or state of being sincere; honesty of mind or intention; freedom from simulation, hypocrisy, disguise, or false pretense; sincereness. I protest, in the sincerity of love. Shak. Sincerity is a duty no less plain than important. Knox.
siva: One of the triad of Hindoo gods. He is the avenger or destroyer, and in modern worship symbolizes the reproductive power of nature.
sirenia: An order of large aquatic herbivorous mammals, including the manatee, dugong, rytina, and several fossil genera. Note: The hind limbs are either rudimentary or wanting, and the front ones are changed to paddles. They have horny plates on the front part of the jaws, and usually flat-crowned molar teeth.
siphonophoran: Belonging to the Siphonophora. -- n. One of the Siphonophora.
sivatherium: A genus of very large extinct ruminants found in the Tertiary formation of India. The snout was prolonged in the form of a proboscis. The male had four horns, the posterior pair being large and branched. It was allied to the antelopes, but very much larger than any exsisting species.
sing: 1. To utter sounds with musical inflections or melodious modulations of voice, as fancy may dictate, or according to the notes of a song or tune, or of a given part (as alto, tenor, etc.) in a chorus… | 1. To utter with musical infections or modulations of voice. And they sing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb. Rev. xv. 3. And in the darkness sing your carol of high…
sinecurism: The state of having a sinecure.
sixteenth: 1. Sixth after the tenth; next in order after the fifteenth. 2. Constituting or being one of sixteen equal parts into which anything is divided. Sixteenth note (Mus.), the sixteenth part of a whole… | 1. The quotient of a unit divided by sixteen; one of sixteen equal parts of one whole. 2. The next in order after the fifteenth; the sixth after the tenth. 3. (Mus.) An interval comprising two…
silt: Mud or fine earth deposited from running or standing water. | To choke, fill, or obstruct with silt or mud.
simile: A word or phrase by which anything is likened, in one or more of its aspects, to something else; a similitude; a poetical or imaginative comparison. A good swift simile, but something currish. Shak.
sickle: 1. A reaping instrument consisting of a steel blade curved into the form of a hook, and having a handle fitted on a tang. The sickle has one side of the blade notched, so as always to sharpen with a serrated edge. Cf. Reaping hook, under Reap. When corn has once felt the sickle, it has no more benefit from the sunshine. Shak. 2.
sike: Such. See Such. (old) "Sike fancies weren foolerie." Spenser. | A gutter; a stream, such as is usually dry in summer. [Prov. Eng. & Scot.]
sidewalk: A walk for foot passengers at the side of a street or road; a foot pavement. [U.S.]
signalment: The act of signaling, or of signalizing; hence, description by peculiar, appropriate, or characteristic marks. Mrs. Browning.
single: 1. One only, as distinguished from more than one; consisting of one alone; individual; separate; as, a single star. No single man is born with a right of controlling the opinions of all the rest. | 1. To select, as an individual person or thing, from among a number; to choose out from others; to separate. Dogs who hereby can single out their master in the dark. Bacon.
signalist: One who makes signals; one who communicates intelligence by means of signals.
sippet: A small sop; a small, thin piece of toasted bread soaked in milk, broth, or the like; a small piece of toasted or fried bread cut into some special shape and used for garnishing. Your sweet sippets in widows' houses. Milton.
six: One more than five; twice three; as, six yards. Six Nations (Ethnol.), a confederation of North American Indians formed by the union of the Tuscaroras and the Five Nations. -- Six points circle. | 1. The number greater by a unit than five; the sum of three and three; six units or objects. 2. A symbol representing six units, as 6, vi., or VI. To be at six and seven or at sixes and sevens, to be…
sitology: A treatise on the regulation of the diet; dietetics. [Written also sitiology.]
silene: A genus of caryophyllaceous plants, usually covered with a viscid secretion by which insects are caught; catchfly. Bon Silène. See Silène, in the Vocabulary.
silesian: Of or pertaining to Silesia. -- n. A native or inhabitant of Silesia.
siphonobranchiate: Having a siphon, or siphons, to convey water to the gills; belonging or pertaining to the Siphonobranchiata. -- n. One of the Siphonobranchiata.
sindon: 1. A wrapper. (old) "Wrapped in sindons of linen." Bacon. 2. (Surg.) A small rag or pledget introduced into the hole in the cranium made by a trephine. Dunglison.
sicca: A seal; a coining die; -- used adjectively to designate the silver currency of the Mogul emperors, or the Indian rupee of 192 grains. Sicca rupee, an East Indian coin, valued nominally at about two shillings sterling, or fifty cents.
sitzbath: A tub in which one bathes in a sitting posture; also, a bath so taken; a hip bath.
siliquosa: A Linnæan order of plants including those which bear siliques.
simple: 1. Single; not complex; not infolded or entangled; uncombined; not compounded; not blended with something else; not complicated; as, a simple substance; a simple idea; a simple sound; | 1. Something not mixed or compounded. "Compounded of many simples." Shak. 2. (Med.) A medicinal plant; -- so called because each vegetable was supposed to possess its particular virtue, and therefore…
singe: 1. To burn slightly or superficially; to burn the surface of; to burn the ends or outside of; as, to singe the hair or the skin. You sulphurous and thought-executing fires, . . . | A burning of the surface; a slight burn.
singult: A sigh or sobbing; also, a hiccough. (old) Spenser. W. Browne.
siluridan: Any fish of the family Silurid or of the order Siluroidei.
sinistrin: A mucilaginous carbohydrate, resembling achroödextrin, extracted from squill as a colorless amorphous substance; -- so called because it is levorotatory.
siphonarid: Any one of numerous species of limpet-shaped pulmonate gastropods of the genus Siphonaria. They cling to rocks between high and low water marks and have both lunglike organs and gills. -- Si`pho*na"rid, a.
sifter: 1. One who, or that which, sifts. 2. (Zoöl.) Any lamellirostral bird, as a duck or goose; -- so called because it sifts or strains its food from the water and mud by means of the lamell
simpleton: A person of weak intellect; a silly person.
sideways: Toward the side; sidewise. A second refraction made sideways. Sir I. Newton. His beard, a good palm's length, at least, . . . Shot sideways, like a swallow's wings. Longfellow.
sicle: A shekel. (old) The holy mother brought five sicles and a pair of turtledoves to redeem the Lamb of God. Jer. Taylor.
singlehearted: Having an honest heart; free from duplicity. -- Sin"gle-heart"ed*ly, adv.
sideling: Sidelong; on the side; laterally; also, obliquely; askew. A fellow nailed up maps . . . some sideling, and others upside down. Swift. | Inclining to one sidel directed toward one side; sloping; inclined; as, sideling ground.
situate: 1. Having a site, situation, or location; being in a relative position; permanently fixed; placed; located; as, a town situated, or situate, on a hill or on the seashore. 2. Placed; residing. Pleasure situate in hill and dale. Milton. Note: Situate is now less used than situated, but both are well authorized.
sitter: 1. One who sits; esp., one who sits for a portrait or a bust. 2. A bird that sits or incubates.
siphonophora: An order of pelagic Hydrozoa including species which form complex free-swimming communities composed of numerous zooids of various kinds, some of which act as floats or as swimming organs, others as feeding or nutritive zooids, and others as reproductive zooids. See Illust. under Physallia, and Porpita.
siphuncular: Of or pertaining to the siphuncle.
singular: 1. Separate or apart from others; single; distinct. (old) Bacon. And God forbid that all a company Should rue a singular man's folly. Chaucer. 2. Engaged in by only one on a side; single. | 1. An individual instance; a particular. (old) Dr. H. More. 2. (Gram) The singular number, or the number denoting one person or thing; a word in the singular number.
siphonopoda: A division of Scaphopoda including those in which the foot terminates in a circular disk.
sinewed: 1. Furnished with sinews; as, a strong-sinewed youth. 2. Fig.: Equipped; strengthened. When he sees Ourselves well sinewed to our defense. Shak.
simonpure: Genuine; true; real; authentic; -- a term alluding to the comedy character Simon Pure, who is impersonated by another and is obliged to prove himself to be the "real Simon Pure."
silly: 1. Happy; fortunate; blessed. (old) Chaucer. 2. Harmless; innocent; inoffensive. (old) "This silly, innocent Custance." Chaucer. The silly virgin strove him to withstand. Spenser. A silly, innocent hare murdered of a dog. Robynson (More's Utopia). 3. Weak; helpless; frail. (old) After long storms . . . With which my silly bark was tossed sore. Spenser.
silent: 1. Free from sound or noise; absolutely still; perfectly quiet. How silent is this town! Shak. 2. Not speaking; indisposed to talk; speechless; mute; taciturn; not loquacious; not talkative. | That which is silent; a time of silence. "The silent of the night." Shak.
singleton: In certain games at cards, as whist, a single card of any suit held at the deal by a player; as, to lead a singleton.
sign: That by which anything is made known or represented; that which furnishes evidence; a mark; a token; an indication; a proof. Specifically: (a) A remarkable event, considered by the ancients as… | 1. To represent by a sign; to make known in a typical or emblematic manner, in distinction from speech; to signify. I signed to Browne to make his retreat. Sir W. Scott. 2. To make a sign upon;
sidewheel: Having a paddle wheel on each side; -- said of steam vessels; as, a side-wheel steamer.
sirius: The Dog Star. See Dog Star.
sizzle: To make a hissing sound; to fry, or to dry and shrivel up, with a hissing sound. [Prov. Eng. & Colloq. U. S.] Forby. | A hissing sound, as of something frying over a fire. [Prov. Eng. & Colloq. U. S.]
sifflement: The act of whistling or hissing; a whistling sound; sibilation. (old) A. Brewer.
sith: Since; afterwards; seeing that. (old) We need not fear them, sith Christ is with us. Latimer. Sith thou art rightful judge. Chaucer. | Time. (old) Chaucer. And humbly thanked him a thousand sithes. Spenser.
silurian: Of or pertaining to the country of the ancient Silures; -- a term applied to the earliest of the Paleozoic eras, and also to the strata of the era, because most plainly developed in that country. Note: The Silurian formation, so named by Murchison, is divided into the Upper Silurian and Lower Silurian.
sideflash: A disruptive discharge between a conductor traversed by an oscillatory current of high frequency (as lightning) and neighboring masses of metal, or between different parts of the same conductor.
sifilet: The six-shafted bird of paradise. See Paradise bird, under Paradise.
sikhs: A religious sect noted for warlike traits, founded in the Punjab at the end of the 15th century.
sinewy: 1. Pertaining to, consisting of, or resembling, a sinew or sinews. The sinewy thread my brain lets fall. Donne. 2. Well braced with, or as if with, sinews; nervous; vigorous; strong; firm; tough; as, the sinewy Ajax. A man whose words . . . were so close and sinewy. Hare.
simpleness: The quality or state of being simple; simplicity. Shak.
siegework: A temporary fort or parallel where siege guns are mounted.
siskin: (a) A small green and yellow European finch (Spinus spinus, or Carduelis spinus); -- called also aberdevine. (b) The American pinefinch (S. pinus); -- called also pine siskin. See Pinefinch. Note: The name is applied also to several other related species found in Asia and South America. Siskin green, a delicate shade of yellowish green, as in the mineral torbernite.
sidle: To go or move with one side foremost; to move sidewise; as, to sidle through a crowd or narrow opening. Swift. He . . . then sidled close to the astonished girl. Sir W. Scott.
simonian: One of the followers of Simon Magus; also, an adherent of certain heretical sects in the early Christian church.
simplify: To make simple; to make less complex; to make clear by giving the explanation for; to show an easier or shorter process for doing or making. The collection of duties is drawn to a point, and so far simplified. A. Hamilton. It is important, in scientific pursuits, to be caitious in simplifying our deductions. W. Nicholson.
sinecure: 1. An ecclesiastical benefice without the care of souls. Ayliffe. 2. Any office or position which requires or involves little or no responsibility, labor, or active service. | To put or place in a sinecure.
sinew: 1. (Anat.) A tendon or tendonous tissue. See Tendon. 2. Muscle; nerve. Sir J. Davies. 3. Fig.: That which supplies strength or power. The portion and sinew of her fortune, her marriage dowry. Shak. | To knit together, or make strong with, or as with, sinews. Shak. Wretches, now stuck up for long tortures . . . might, if properly treated, serve to sinew the state in time of danger. Goldsmith.
sile: To strain, as fresh milk. [Prov. Eng.] | To drop; to flow; to fall. [Prov. Eng.]
sider: One who takes a side. | Cider. (old)
silurus: A genus of large malacopterygious fishes of the order Siluroidei. They inhabit the inland waters of Europe and Asia.
sinapisin: A substance extracted from mustard seed and probably identical with sinalbin. (old)
siriasis: (a) A sunstroke. (b) The act of exposing to a sun bath. (old) Cf. Insolation.
sibylline: Pertaining to the sibyls; uttered, written, or composed by sibyls; like the productions of sibyls. Sibylline books. (a) (Rom. Antiq.) Books or documents of prophecies in verse concerning the fate of the Roman empire, said to have been purchased by Tarquin the Proud from a sibyl.
signior: Sir; Mr. The English form and pronunciation for the Italian Signor and the Spanish Señor.
sieve: 1. A utensil for separating the finer and coarser parts of a pulverized or granulated substance from each other. It consist of a vessel, usually shallow, with the bottom perforated, or made of hair, wire, or the like, woven in meshes. "In a sieve thrown and sifted." Chaucer. 2. A kind of coarse basket. Simmonds. Sieve cells (Bot.), cribriform cells. See under Cribriform.
siliquiform: Having the form of a silique.
siphonium: A bony tube which, in some birds, connects the tympanium with the air chambers of the articular piece of the mandible.
sigillarid: One of an extinct family of cryptagamous trees, including the genus Sigillaria and its allies.
silverware: Dishes, vases, ornaments, and utensils of various sorts, made of silver.
similitude: 1. The quality or state of being similar or like; resemblance; likeness; similarity; as, similitude of substance. Chaucer. Let us make now man in our image, man In our similitude. Milton. If fate some future bard shall join In sad similitude of griefs to mine. Pope. 2. The act of likening, or that which likens, one thing to another; fanciful or imaginative comparison;
siss: To make a hissing sound; as, a flatiron hot enough to siss when touched with a wet finger. [Colloq. U. S.; Local, Eng.] | A hissing noise. [Colloq. U. S.]
sixshooter: A pistol or other firearm which can be fired six times without reloading especially, a six-chambered revolver. [Colloq. U.S.]
siliquous: Bearing siliques; as, siliquose plants; pertaining to, or resembling, siliques; as, siliquose capsules.
sik: Such. See Such. (old) "Sike fancies weren foolerie." Spenser.
signality: The quality or state of being signal or remarkable. (old) Sir T. Browne.
sithence: Since. See Sith, and Sithen. (old) Piers Plowman.
simnel: 1. A kind of cake made of fine flour; a cracknel. (old) Not common bread, but vastel bread, or simnels. Fuller. 2. A kind of rich plum cake, eaten especially on Mid-Lent Sunday. [Eng.] Herrick.
sibilant: Making a hissing sound; uttered with a hissing sound; hissing; as, s, z, sh, and zh, are sibilant elementary sounds. -- n. A sibiliant letter.
singularist: One who affects singularity. (old) A clownish singularist, or nonconformist to ordinary usage. Borrow.
situation: 1. Manner in which an object is placed; location, esp. as related to something else; position; locality site; as, a house in a pleasant situation. 2.
